name: High blood pressure (hypertension)
overview: High blood pressure means the force of blood against the artery walls is consistently too high. It rarely causes symptoms, so the only way to know is to have it measured. Left untreated it raises the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney disease, but lifestyle changes and medicines can control it.
symptoms: Very high blood pressure can occasionally cause headaches, blurred vision or chest pain
causes: Often no single cause, but linked to lifestyle and genes
Being overweight, eating too much salt and not exercising enough
Drinking too much alcohol and smoking
Some conditions such as kidney disease, or certain medicines
riskFactors: Family history of high blood pressure
Being of Black African or Black Caribbean descent
High-salt diet, low physical activity, alcohol and smoking
diagnosis: Blood pressure is measured with a cuff on several occasions; home or 24-hour ambulatory monitoring is often used to confirm the diagnosis.
treatment: Lifestyle changes: less salt, healthy diet, more activity, less alcohol, stopping smoking
Blood pressure-lowering medicines prescribed by a doctor
Regular blood pressure checks
selfCare: Check blood pressure at home if advised
prevention: Healthy, balanced diet with plenty of fruit and vegetables
Regular blood pressure checks, especially over 40
whenToSeeDoctor: You are over 40 and have not had your blood pressure checked recently
Home readings are consistently high
Side effects from blood pressure medicines
emergencySigns: Very high reading with chest pain, shortness of breath or severe headache
Signs of stroke: face drooping, arm weakness or speech problems
Sudden changes in vision or confusion

name: High cholesterol
overview: Cholesterol is a fatty substance in the blood. Too much of it can build up in the arteries and raise the risk of heart attack and stroke. It does not usually cause symptoms and is found with a blood test.
symptoms: It is often found only through a blood test or after a heart attack or stroke
Very high inherited cholesterol can occasionally cause fatty lumps on tendons or yellowish patches around the eyes
causes: Eating a lot of saturated fat
Not exercising enough, being overweight, smoking and drinking alcohol
Inherited conditions such as familial hypercholesterolaemia
Other conditions such as diabetes, kidney disease or an underactive thyroid
riskFactors: Family history of high cholesterol or early heart disease
diagnosis: High cholesterol is diagnosed with a blood test, often as part of a routine health check alongside an assessment of overall heart risk.
treatment: Diet and lifestyle changes
Cholesterol-lowering medicines such as statins, prescribed by a doctor
Treating linked conditions such as diabetes
selfCare: Eat less saturated fat and more fibre, fruit, vegetables and oily fish
prevention: Regular checks if you are at higher risk
whenToSeeDoctor: You are over 40 and have not had a cholesterol test
A family history of high cholesterol or early heart disease
You are overweight or have diabetes or high blood pressure
emergencySigns: Chest pain or pressure, which could be a heart attack
Sudden face drooping, arm weakness or speech problems (possible stroke)

name: Coronary heart disease
overview: Coronary heart disease happens when the arteries supplying the heart become narrowed by fatty deposits. It can cause chest pain (angina) and heart attacks. It cannot be cured, but treatment and lifestyle changes can greatly reduce the risk.
symptoms: Chest pain or tightness (angina), often brought on by exertion or stress
Pain in the arm, neck, jaw, back or stomach
Some people have no symptoms before a heart attack
causes: Build-up of fatty material in the walls of the coronary arteries (atherosclerosis)
Damage to arteries from smoking, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and diabetes
diagnosis: Doctors use a risk assessment, blood tests, an ECG, and tests such as an exercise test, CT scan or coronary angiogram.
treatment: Medicines to reduce symptoms and risk of heart attack, prescribed by a doctor
Procedures to widen arteries (angioplasty and stents)
Coronary artery bypass surgery
Cardiac rehabilitation
selfCare: Eat a healthy diet and be physically active
Keep blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes under control
Carry any prescribed angina spray and know how to use it
prevention: Managing blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes
whenToSeeDoctor: Chest pain or tightness that comes on with activity and settles with rest
Increasing breathlessness
Angina that is happening more often or with less effort
emergencySigns: Chest pain that is sudden, severe or lasts more than a few minutes, or does not settle with rest or your angina medicine
Chest pain spreading to the arms, neck, jaw or back
Chest pain with sweating, breathlessness or feeling sick

name: Heart attack
overview: A heart attack is a medical emergency where the blood supply to part of the heart is suddenly blocked, usually by a blood clot. Calling emergency services immediately saves lives and heart muscle. Treatment and rehabilitation help people recover and prevent another attack.
symptoms: Chest pain: pressure, tightness or squeezing in the centre of the chest
Pain spreading to the arms, neck, jaw, back or tummy
causes: Usually coronary heart disease, where a fatty plaque in an artery bursts and a clot forms
Less commonly, a spasm or tear in a coronary artery
riskFactors: High blood pressure, high cholesterol and diabetes
diagnosis: A heart attack is diagnosed in hospital with an ECG and blood tests that measure heart muscle damage.
treatment: Emergency treatment to restore blood flow, such as a stent procedure or clot-dissolving medicine
Medicines to protect the heart and prevent another heart attack
Cardiac rehabilitation programme
selfCare: Call emergency services straight away if you suspect a heart attack
While waiting, sit down and rest; chew aspirin only if advised by the call handler and not allergic
Take part in cardiac rehabilitation after a heart attack
prevention: Healthy diet, weight and regular activity
Control blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes
whenToSeeDoctor: Chest discomfort that comes and goes with activity (possible angina)
After a heart attack, any new or worsening symptoms
emergencySigns: Chest pain or pressure that does not go away
Chest pain with breathlessness, sweating or feeling sick
Pain spreading to the arm, jaw, neck or back
Collapse or unconsciousness

name: Heart failure
overview: Heart failure means the heart is not pumping blood around the body as well as it should. It is a long-term condition that usually gets worse over time, but treatment can control symptoms for many years and help people live well.
symptoms: Breathlessness after activity or at rest
Feeling tired most of the time
Breathlessness when lying down or waking at night breathless
causes: Coronary heart disease and previous heart attacks
High blood pressure
Problems with heart muscle (cardiomyopathy) or heart valves
Irregular heart rhythms such as atrial fibrillation
riskFactors: Coronary heart disease or past heart attack
diagnosis: Heart failure is diagnosed with blood tests, an ECG and an echocardiogram (heart ultrasound).
treatment: Medicines to help the heart work better and reduce fluid build-up
Devices such as pacemakers or implantable defibrillators in some people
Surgery or procedures for valve or artery problems
Heart failure rehabilitation
selfCare: Weigh yourself daily if advised, as sudden gain can mean fluid build-up
Limit salt and alcohol and stop smoking
prevention: Treat coronary heart disease risk factors
whenToSeeDoctor: Persistent breathlessness or tiredness
Swollen ankles or legs
Symptoms getting worse if you already have heart failure
Rapid weight gain over a few days
emergencySigns: Severe breathlessness or struggling to breathe
Chest pain
Coughing up frothy pink mucus
Fainting or collapse

name: Atrial fibrillation
overview: Atrial fibrillation is a common heart rhythm problem that causes an irregular and often fast heartbeat. It raises the risk of stroke because blood clots can form in the heart. Treatment controls the heart rate or rhythm and lowers stroke risk.
symptoms: Tiredness and less able to exercise
causes: High blood pressure
Coronary heart disease, heart failure or heart valve problems
Overactive thyroid
Heavy alcohol use
Sometimes no clear cause
diagnosis: AF is diagnosed with an electrocardiogram (ECG), sometimes using a portable monitor worn for a day or longer.
treatment: Anticoagulant medicines to reduce the risk of stroke
Medicines to control heart rate or rhythm
Cardioversion (a controlled electric shock) to reset the rhythm
Catheter ablation in some people
selfCare: Limit alcohol and caffeine if they trigger symptoms
Keep to a healthy weight and be active
whenToSeeDoctor: Your heartbeat feels irregular or very fast
Palpitations with dizziness or breathlessness
An irregular pulse found on a smartwatch or home check
emergencySigns: Chest pain
Severe breathlessness
Fainting or collapse
Signs of stroke: face drooping, arm weakness, speech problems

name: Stroke
overview: A stroke is a medical emergency where the blood supply to part of the brain is cut off, by a clot or by bleeding. The faster treatment starts, the less damage there is. A transient ischaemic attack (TIA or mini-stroke) has similar symptoms that pass, but is a warning that needs urgent assessment.
symptoms: Face drooping on one side or unable to smile
Weakness or numbness in one arm or leg
Sudden loss of vision, dizziness or loss of balance
causes: A blood clot blocking an artery to the brain (ischaemic stroke)
Bleeding in or around the brain (haemorrhagic stroke)
diagnosis: A stroke is diagnosed in hospital with an urgent brain scan (CT or MRI) and other tests to find the cause.
treatment: Clot-busting medicine or clot removal for ischaemic stroke, if given quickly enough
Medicines to prevent further strokes
Surgery for some bleeds
Rehabilitation: physiotherapy, speech and occupational therapy
selfCare: Use the FAST test and call emergency services immediately
Take part in rehabilitation and take prevention medicines as prescribed
whenToSeeDoctor: Stroke-like symptoms that went away (possible TIA) need urgent same-day assessment
Risk factors such as high blood pressure or an irregular pulse
emergencySigns: Face drooping
Arm or leg weakness
Speech problems
Sudden loss of vision, balance or a sudden very severe headache

name: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT)
overview: A DVT is a blood clot in a deep vein, usually in the leg. It can be serious because part of the clot can break off and travel to the lungs (pulmonary embolism). It is treated with medicines that stop clots growing.
symptoms: Throbbing or cramping pain in one leg, usually the calf or thigh
Warm skin around the painful area
Red or darker skin around the painful area
Swollen, hard veins that are sore to touch
causes: Slow or reduced blood flow in the deep veins, for example during long periods of immobility
Damage to a vein wall, such as from surgery or injury
Blood that clots more easily than usual, due to pregnancy, hormones, cancer or inherited conditions
riskFactors: Being immobile, such as after surgery, in hospital or on long journeys
Combined contraceptive pill or hormone therapy
diagnosis: A DVT is diagnosed with a blood test (D-dimer) and an ultrasound scan of the leg.
treatment: Anticoagulant medicines to stop the clot growing
Compression stockings may be advised for symptoms
Occasionally procedures to remove the clot
prevention: Keep moving during long journeys and after surgery
Drink fluids and avoid long periods of sitting
Follow hospital advice on clot prevention
Stop smoking and keep to a healthy weight
whenToSeeDoctor: Pain and swelling in one leg (get help urgently, the same day)
Symptoms in a leg after surgery, a long journey or during pregnancy
emergencySigns: Sudden breathlessness
Chest pain, especially when breathing in
Coughing up blood
Fast heartbeat or collapse

name: Pulmonary embolism
overview: A pulmonary embolism is a blockage of a blood vessel in the lungs, usually by a clot that has travelled from the leg. It can be life-threatening and needs urgent treatment.
symptoms: Chest pain, especially when breathing in
Pain and swelling in a leg (from a DVT)
causes: A blood clot, usually from a deep vein in the leg (DVT), travelling to the lungs
Rarely, a blockage from fat, air or other material entering the bloodstream
riskFactors: Combined hormonal contraception or hormone therapy
diagnosis: A PE is diagnosed in hospital with blood tests and scans such as a CT pulmonary angiogram or a lung scan.
treatment: Anticoagulant medicines
Clot-dissolving medicine or procedures in severe cases
Hospital monitoring
selfCare: Stay active as advised during recovery
prevention: Clot prevention measures after surgery or in hospital
whenToSeeDoctor: Breathlessness or chest pain after recent surgery or immobility: seek urgent help
Pain and swelling in one leg, which may be a DVT that could lead to PE
New or worsening symptoms while on treatment
emergencySigns: Sudden breathlessness
Chest pain when breathing in
Coughing up blood
Collapse

name: Varicose veins
overview: Varicose veins are swollen, twisted veins, usually in the legs, caused by weak valves in the veins. They are common and often harmless, though they can ache or itch. Treatment is usually only needed if they cause problems.
symptoms: Blue or dark purple, bulging, twisted veins
Burning or throbbing in the legs
Dry, itchy skin over the vein
causes: Weak or damaged valves inside the veins that let blood flow backwards and collect
Increased pressure in the leg veins, for example from pregnancy, overweight or long periods of standing
riskFactors: Jobs involving long periods of standing
diagnosis: A GP diagnoses varicose veins by looking at the legs; an ultrasound scan may be done if treatment is considered.
treatment: Compression stockings
Procedures such as heat or laser treatment to seal veins
Injections to close veins (sclerotherapy)
Surgery to remove veins in some cases
selfCare: Avoid standing still for long periods
prevention: Avoid standing or sitting for long periods without moving
whenToSeeDoctor: Veins are painful or causing discomfort
Skin over the veins is changing colour, sore or itchy
Veins become hot, red and painful (possible inflammation)
emergencySigns: A vein that is bleeding heavily and does not stop with pressure
Sudden leg swelling and pain with breathlessness or chest pain

name: Peripheral arterial disease (PAD)
overview: Peripheral arterial disease is a narrowing of the arteries that carry blood to the legs, caused by fatty deposits. It is a sign of a higher risk of heart attack and stroke. Lifestyle changes, exercise and medicines can help.
symptoms: Painful cramping in the hips, thighs or calves when walking, which eases with rest
Hair loss on the legs and feet
Numbness or weakness in the legs
Shiny skin or skin colour changes on the legs
Sores on the feet or legs that do not heal
causes: Build-up of fatty deposits in the leg arteries (atherosclerosis)
Artery damage made worse by smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol
diagnosis: PAD is usually diagnosed by comparing blood pressure in the ankles and arms (ankle-brachial index), sometimes followed by an ultrasound scan.
treatment: Stopping smoking and supervised exercise programmes
Medicines to lower cholesterol, control blood pressure and reduce clotting
Angioplasty or bypass surgery in severe cases
selfCare: Look after your feet and check them daily
prevention: Control diabetes, blood pressure and cholesterol
whenToSeeDoctor: Leg pain when walking that goes away with rest
Sores on the legs or feet that do not heal
Cold, numb or discoloured legs or feet
emergencySigns: A suddenly cold, pale, painful, numb leg or foot
Black or dying skin on the toes or foot

name: Asthma
overview: Asthma is a common long-term condition where the airways become inflamed and narrow, making it hard to breathe at times. It usually starts in childhood but can begin at any age. With the right treatment most people can control their symptoms well.
symptoms: Coughing, often worse at night or early morning
causes: Inflamed, sensitive airways that react to triggers
Triggers such as colds, allergies (pollen, dust mites, pets), smoke, exercise, cold air and air pollution
riskFactors: Family history of asthma or allergies
Low birth weight or premature birth
Work exposure to dusts or chemicals
diagnosis: Asthma is diagnosed from symptoms and breathing tests such as spirometry, peak flow monitoring or a FeNO test.
treatment: Inhalers: relievers to ease symptoms and preventers to reduce airway inflammation
Combination inhalers
Tablets or other medicines if inhalers alone do not control symptoms
A personal asthma action plan
selfCare: Use inhalers as prescribed and check your technique
Know and avoid your triggers where possible
prevention: Take preventer medicine regularly if prescribed
Get flu and other recommended vaccines
whenToSeeDoctor: You think you or your child may have asthma
You need your reliever inhaler 3 or more times a week
Symptoms wake you at night
Your asthma is affecting daily life
emergencySigns: Reliever inhaler is not helping
Too breathless to speak, eat or sleep
Breathing getting faster and you cannot catch your breath
Lips or fingers turning blue or grey
Drowsiness or confusion

name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
overview: COPD is a long-term lung condition, including emphysema and chronic bronchitis, that makes it harder to breathe. It is mostly caused by smoking and gets slowly worse over time. Treatment and stopping smoking can slow it down and help people stay active.
causes: Smoking, the main cause
Long-term exposure to fumes, dust or air pollution
Rarely, an inherited condition called alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
riskFactors: Indoor smoke from cooking or heating fuels
diagnosis: COPD is diagnosed with a breathing test called spirometry, along with a chest X-ray and blood tests to rule out other causes.
treatment: Stopping smoking
Inhalers to open the airways
Pulmonary rehabilitation (an exercise and education programme)
Tablets, oxygen therapy or surgery in some cases
selfCare: Have a rescue plan for flare-ups
prevention: Avoid workplace dust and fumes with proper protection
Flu, pneumococcal and other recommended vaccines
whenToSeeDoctor: Persistent breathlessness, cough or wheeze
Frequent chest infections
Symptoms getting worse over days (a flare-up)
emergencySigns: Severe breathlessness that is not relieved by usual treatment
Lips or skin turning blue or grey
Confusion or drowsiness
Chest pain

name: Obstructive sleep apnoea
overview: Obstructive sleep apnoea is when the throat walls relax and narrow during sleep, interrupting breathing. It causes loud snoring and daytime sleepiness. Treatment can improve sleep and lower risks such as high blood pressure and accidents.
symptoms: Breathing stopping and starting during sleep (often noticed by a partner)
Loud snoring, gasping or choking noises
Feeling very sleepy during the day
causes: The muscles and soft tissue in the throat relaxing and narrowing the airway during sleep
Extra tissue around the neck or a narrow airway, for example from overweight or large tonsils
riskFactors: Drinking alcohol or taking sedatives before bed
Enlarged tonsils or a small jaw
diagnosis: Sleep apnoea is diagnosed with a sleep study, often using a device worn at home overnight that measures breathing and oxygen levels.
treatment: Lifestyle changes such as weight loss and less alcohol
A CPAP machine that gently pumps air through a mask during sleep
A mouth device (mandibular advancement device) for some people
Surgery is rarely needed
selfCare: Avoid alcohol and sleeping pills before bed
whenToSeeDoctor: Someone notices you stop breathing or gasp while asleep
You feel very tired during the day despite sleeping
You fall asleep at inappropriate times, such as while driving
emergencySigns: Chest pain or severe breathlessness
Being extremely drowsy and hard to wake
